title: Pfand, Kilo und der Supermarkt
summary: Shopping at Rewe or Aldi, naming quantities, and the German bottle-deposit system (Pfand)

blocks.title: Rewe, Aldi und das Kassenband
blocks.body: German supermarkets (**Rewe, Aldi, Lidl**) run fast. Cashiers scan at lightning speed, so you bag your own groceries — quickly, usually standing right at the belt. Bring your own bag, or buy a **Tüte** for a small fee. Quantities are metric: **ein Kilo**, **200 Gramm**, **ein Liter**, **eine Packung**.
blocks.callout: Tip: watch the belt, not your phone — the cashier will beat you to the end of it.

blocks.title: Pfand — dein Geld kommt zurück
blocks.body: Most bottles and cans in Germany carry **Pfand** — a small deposit added to the price. Bring the empty back to the **Pfandautomat** (the reverse-vending machine, usually near the entrance), feed it in, and get a receipt worth a few cents each. Skipping it is basically leaving coins on the floor.
blocks.callout: *Ist da Pfand drauf?* — "Is there a deposit on that?" — a very normal question to ask.

pairs.left: die Mehrwegflasche — reusable bottle, washed and refilled
pairs.right: die Einwegflasche — single-use bottle, recycled after Pfand return
pairs.note: Both carry Pfand; the difference is what happens after you return it.

blocks.prompt: You finish a bottle of water with Pfand on it. What do you do?
options: Throw it in the normal trash
Bring it to the Pfandautomat for money back
blocks.explain: *Pfandautomat* — feed the empty in, get a receipt, and the deposit comes back at the register.

blocks.prompt: Type the shopping-list line: '200 grams of cheese'.
blocks.hint: Gramm doesn't take a plural -s here.
blocks.explain: *200 Gramm Käse* — German quantities sit straight in front of the noun, no 'of' needed.
